children: Earlier this month, my wife and I were on a visit to Vienna. One of the things we did there was attend a Mozart concert. Vienna is the city where Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart lived and worked, two centuries ago. It was also home to other legendary music composers such as Beethoven, Brahms and Schubert. Little wonder the city is called the capital of western classical music.

The Mozart concert we attended was at the grand Golden Hall of Musikverein, one of Vienna’s most beautiful musical performance venues. The ornate hall was packed. The audience went into raptures as Mozart’s symphonies wove their magical notes all around us. It was such a beautiful evening.

The concert set me thinking about how western classical music has been used by brands across the world. The first brand that came to my mind, quite naturally, was one with which I have worked for several years — Titan watches.

When Titan watches were first launched in India in the late 1980s, the signature music used in its advertising was Mozart’s 25th symphony. This was an audacious decision, given that few Indians follow western classical music. Yet it worked brilliantly. Mozart’s music entered millions of Indian homes, and the symphony soon became identified as the Titan tune. Forty years later, it remains popular.

The credit should go to Suresh Mullick, the creative head of Ogilvy (then called O&M), and Xerxes Desai, the founder-managing director of Titan Company. They felt the music best captured the uplifting emotion, precision and global aspiration inherent in Titan watches.

I remember receiving a Mont Blanc pen as a gift from a friend many years ago. The special-edition pen was a tribute to Mozart. The pen’s lovely black resin was adorned with elegant platinum details. The Mozart connection? An accompanying compact disc of his music. I treasure the pen till date.
McDonald’s, the fast-food brand, has used Mozart’s music in its advertising to create an interesting contrast between everyday relaxed food moments and the solemn grandeur of classical music.

At the opposite end of calm, there is the intensity of Mozart. Nike has used one of the most dramatic movements in Mozart’s music — the Lacrimosa from his Requiem — to highlight the vigour of athletic endeavours.
Hyundai, LG and Amazon have used Mozart’s tunes too.
Why do so many brands leverage the music and memory of a man who lived more than 250 years ago?
First and foremost, brands try to evoke emotions in the minds of consumers. Mozart’s music evokes a cadence of emotions — from joy to grief, calm to longing, playfulness to solemnity.
Second, classical music brings with it the grandeur and sophistication that many brands desire to project.

Contrast this with the easy listening charms of Bollywood, the warmth of jazz or the introspective moods of ghazals. Discerning brands choose the music that matches the personalities they wish to project.

Finally, so much of classical music is timeless and appeals across ages. At the Vienna concert, the audience was a balanced mix of Gen Z, middle-aged and silver-haired people — all lost in the music, enjoying it thoroughly. That’s the power of Mozart.

title: The curious marketer. Brands that scored with Mozart’s amazing symphonies
